A1-A2.headline: The Famous Historic House in Frankfurt Old Town

pages.text: Have you ever seen a house that was destroyed and then built again? In Frankfurt, there is a famous old timber house called the Haus zur Goldenen Waage. It is a beautiful piece of history that stands in the city center today.
pages.caption: Reconstruction of the Goldenen Waage in January 2018

evidence.articleCaption: Reconstruction of the Goldenen Waage in January 2018

pages.text: Long ago, in 1323, people first wrote about this house. It had many names and owners over the years. In 1588, Andreas Gaßmann bought the property. Later, in 1605, a spice trader named Abraham van Hamel bought it too. These owners helped make the house a special place in the city. It was a busy spot for trade and life in the old town of Frankfurt.

In 2014, workers started a big project to rebuild the house. They wanted it to look just like it did in the past. By 2017, the work was finished. The house is now a beautiful landmark in Frankfurt. It shows us how the old town used to look. Many people visit the square to see the timber facade and the roof. It is a great way to learn about the history of the city.

The house was destroyed in a war air raid in 1944. It was a very sad time for the city. But now, the house is back. It stands tall near the cathedral. Visitors love to walk by and see the history. It is a reminder of the past and a symbol of the city's future. The house is a special place for everyone in Frankfurt to enjoy and remember.

B1-B2.headline: Rebuilding the Historic Haus zur Goldenen Waage in Frankfurt

pages.text: What happens when a historic city loses its most beautiful building? In Frankfurt, the Haus zur Goldenen Waage was lost in wartime, but it has returned to grace the city center once again.
pages.caption: Reconstruction of the Goldenen Waage.

evidence.fileTitle: File:Frankfurt Goldene Waage Januar 2018 Ansicht vom Domplatz.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Reconstruction of the Goldenen Waage in January 2018

pages.text: Historical records first mention the property in 1323. By 1588, Andreas Gaßmann had purchased the corner house. Soon after, in 1605, a spice trader named Abraham van Hamel acquired the building. Hamel had big plans for the site, intending to transform the structure into a grand home that would reflect his success and status in the busy market district of Frankfurt.

Hamel wanted a magnificent Renaissance facade, which was built in 1619. However, his ambitious plans caused strong opposition from neighbors and local councils. They worried about street width, light, and fire safety. These people felt that a wealthy foreigner should not be allowed to build such a tall house in a narrow alley, leading to many heated arguments and legal disputes.

Decades after its destruction in 1944, modern restoration began in 2014 as part of the Dom-Römer Project. By late 2017, the timber facade and decorative ceiling were completed, reviving a lost architectural piece. Today, the house stands as a proud reminder of Frankfurt's history, showing how careful work can bring the past back to life for future generations to enjoy.

C1-C2.headline: Architectural Heritage and Legal Disputes of the Goldenen Waage

pages.text: The Haus zur Goldenen Waage stands as a celebrated medieval half-timbered structure in Frankfurt, tragically obliterated during the March 1944 air raid. Its architectural significance cemented its status as a prominent urban landmark.
pages.caption: Reconstruction view of the landmark.

evidence.fileTitle: File:Frankfurt Goldene Waage Januar 2018 Ansicht vom Domplatz.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Reconstruction of the Goldenen Waage in January 2018

pages.text: Documented since 1323, the property underwent various amalgamations. In 1588, Andreas Gaßmann secured the site, and in 1605, Abraham van Hamel acquired the estate. Hamel subsequently commissioned a striking Renaissance facade, which was completed around 1619. His investment reflected the commercial prosperity of the era, though it also marked the beginning of significant local tensions regarding urban development.

Hamel's construction endeavors provoked severe friction with patrician neighbors and city authorities. Critics argued that his ostentatious design infringed upon spatial regulations and exacerbated fire hazards in the narrow alleys. Litigation ensued over structural dimensions, culminating in financial penalties for blueprint infractions, as Hamel sought to maximize his property's utility despite significant social and legal resistance.

Following decades of post-war neglect after the 1944 air raid, the Dom-Römer Project spearheaded an authentic reconstruction beginning in 2014. This effort successfully restored the historic facade and interior elements by 2017. The building now serves as a testament to Frankfurt's commitment to preserving its architectural heritage, balancing historical accuracy with the demands of modern urban life.
